kb.title: Arun Velasco
kb.tagline: Payments engineer. Eleven years, four employers, one gap I'll tell you about.

sections.title: Timeline — eleven years, four employers, one gap
sections.summary: The full employment history in order, including the eleven-month gap in 2016, stated plainly rather than smoothed over.
sections.body_md:
**Halberd Systems** — Graduate Engineer — Mar 2012 to Nov 2014. Java, Oracle, internal reporting for an equipment-leasing business. Learned to read a query plan. Left because the team was wound down, with eight months' notice.

**Speedwell Logistics** — Backend Engineer — Jan 2015 to Feb 2016. Route planning and driver dispatch in Python and Postgres. First service he owned that woke him up, and the first time he put a queue in Postgres rather than asking for Kafka.

**Career gap** — Feb 2016 to Jan 2017, eleven months. His father had a stroke and he moved back to Penang to deal with hospitals and insurers. He is explicit that there was no side project and no sabbatical framing: *"I read a lot and I was tired."* It is on the CV in plain text deliberately.

**Rialto Payments** — Senior Backend Engineer — Feb 2017 to Aug 2019. Card acquiring for small merchants: authorisation, capture, refunds, chargeback representment. Also the only machine learning he has shipped — see `ml/currency`.

**Agoda** — Senior, then Staff Engineer — Sep 2019 to Apr 2025. Five and a half years on supplier payouts. Owned virtual card issuance, PSP routing and failover, nightly reconciliation, and the payout queue.

**Independent** — May 2025 to present. Contract backend work and an unpaid advisory seat at NodusArt.

sections.title: Why he left Agoda
sections.summary: One paragraph, no wandering: the platform reached the state he wanted, the remaining work was operating it, and a 2025 reorg pointed at breadth he did not believe in.
sections.body_md:
The payouts platform got to the state he wanted it in — breakers, a `deferred` state, reconciliation with four classes and a ~94% auto-resolve rate, a queue that had not paged anyone in about eight months. What was left was operating it, and he says plainly that he is not the person who enjoys the fourth year of operating something.

A reorg in early 2025 moved the platform under a group whose roadmap was "more surface area, less depth, a lot of integrations" — a direction he did not believe in. He gave three months' notice and left in April 2025.

He is emphatic that nobody was unkind, he was not managed out, and there is no story underneath the one he tells.

sections.title: What he wants next, what he'd turn down, and his band
sections.summary: Correctness-hard payments or ledger work, end-to-end ownership including on-call, staff scope with no management track — plus the roles he would decline and the compensation band, stated up front.
sections.body_md:
**Looking for**

- A payments or ledger system where **correctness is the hard part**, not throughput. Explicitly not an ads pipeline.
- Ownership of something end to end, **including the on-call for it**. He does not want to be handed a service someone else designed and be accountable for its uptime.
- Somewhere he can write at length about the systems he builds — every write-up in this knowledge base was a document he wrote at work first.
- **Staff-level scope without a management track.** He has managed people, was competent at it, and does not want to do it again.

**Would turn down**

- A pure platform-migration role. "A real job and it is not mine."
- A role where the payments logic lives in a vendor and the job is configuring it: *"if nobody on the team can explain what happens on a failed capture, I am support staff with a better title."*
- Anything requiring him to call himself an ML engineer.
- A rate below his band.

**Band, stated in the first conversation on purpose:** 8,000–9,500 USD per month for remote contract work; 4.2–5.0 million THB per year for a permanent role in Bangkok. He says directly that he will not be talked up from it later.

sections.title: Supplier payouts — the issuance flow end to end
sections.summary: Five hops from booking event to settlement: payable created, batched into a payout, PSP selected, virtual card issued, settled and reconciled. Roughly two million payables a month across ~140 countries.
sections.body_md:
Paying hotels rather than taking money from travellers — the mirror image of acquiring, and the failure modes do not rhyme. *"In acquiring, the worst case is you did not get paid. In payouts, the worst case is you paid twice, and the counterparty has no incentive to tell you."*

Scale when he left: roughly two million payables a month, ~140 countries.

1. **Payable created.** A booking event lands; contract terms decide when it falls due. A row with amount, currency, due date and supplier. Nothing moves.
2. **Batched into a payout.** A sweep groups payables by supplier and currency, so a supplier owed eleven small amounts gets one card, not eleven.
3. **PSP selected.** Routing picks a provider for the corridor — currency, country, amount band, and current health. See `agoda/psp-routing#circuit-breakers`.
4. **Virtual card issued.** A single-use card number with an exact limit and a merchant-category lock. The card *is* the payment instrument.
5. **Settlement and reconciliation.** The issuer reports what was actually authorised and captured — rarely instantly, and frequently not equal to what was issued. See `agoda/reconciliation#spark-pipeline`.

sections.title: Virtual card issuance
sections.summary: Real card issuing experience, scoped honestly: single-use virtual commercial cards for B2B payout, not consumer credit. Exact limits, MCC locks, validity windows, fixed currency, across three issuing APIs behind one deliberately narrow interface.
sections.body_md:
He has issued cards, and he scopes it before it can be assumed broader: **single-use virtual commercial cards for B2B payout**, not consumer credit cards.

- **Limits are exact, not approximate.** The card is minted with an authorisation limit equal to the payable, in the payable's currency, and declines anything above it. *"A card with a rounded-up limit is an invitation for a supplier to help themselves."*
- **Merchant category locks.** Lodging MCCs only. Caught real misuse twice that he knows of.
- **Validity windows.** Open at issue, closed on a schedule matching the contract, so an unused card does not sit live for a year.
- **Single use means single use.** A card authorised once is closed to further authorisations even if the amount came in under the limit; the difference is settled through reconciliation, not by leaving the card open.
- **Currency fixed at issuance.** No provider-side conversion — *"a provider's FX spread is not a cost I can explain to finance six weeks later."*

Three PSPs, three issuing APIs, one internal interface — built as **the intersection of what all three could do, not the union**. Every time a single provider's special capability leaked into the interface, it was paid for in the failover path.

sections.title: Idempotency for money movement
sections.summary: The key is derived from (payout_id, attempt_number), generated and persisted before the provider call. Deterministic so a retry reproduces it, durable so it survives process death.
sections.body_md:
Issuing a card is issuing money. The system must never issue two cards for one payable because a call timed out and something retried.

The key is derived from **`(payout_id, attempt_number)`**, and both properties are load-bearing:

- **Deterministic.** Not a UUID per request. A UUID means a retry generates a *new* key, which is identical to having no key. The same logical attempt must produce the same key both times, and deriving it from data that already exists is the only guarantee of that.
- **Generated and persisted before the call goes out.** Written to the database in the same transaction that marks the attempt started, and only then does the provider get called. If the process dies between the write and the response, recovery reads the key back and asks the provider what became of it — impossible if the key only ever existed in memory.

`attempt_number` rather than a bare `payout_id` because a *deliberate* second attempt — first provider hard-declined, trying another — is a genuinely different payment and must not be deduplicated against the first.

His line for juniors: **"an idempotency key that does not survive process death is decoration. Most of the ones I have reviewed are decoration."**

sections.title: PSP circuit breakers, and the incident that reshaped them
sections.summary: One breaker per PSP per corridor. Opens on five consecutive failures or a >20% error rate over sixty seconds; half-open admits exactly one real payout. The PSP-B incident showed the breaker measured the wrong thing, so latency became an input.
sections.body_md:
One breaker **per PSP per corridor**, not per PSP — provider B being broken for THB says little about provider B for EUR, and collapsing them lets one bad corridor take out a healthy one.

**Opens on five consecutive failures, or a greater-than-20% error rate over a sixty-second window**, whichever comes first. Five-in-a-row is the fast path for a provider that has fallen over; the rate-over-window is the slow path for intermittent failure, where you would otherwise wait forever for five consecutive.

**Half-open:** after thirty seconds, exactly one request is admitted — a real payout, not a synthetic ping, because *"a synthetic health check tells you the provider's status page is up, which is not the question."* Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it and doubles the window, capped at five minutes. One request rather than a percentage, because at this volume "let 5% through" sends thousands of real payouts at a provider just judged broken.

**Before the breakers**, provider A returned 503s for forty minutes; retries on a fixed schedule kept the queue saturated and healthy corridors backed up behind it. Nothing was lost — it was slow and obviously preventable, and it bought the budget to build breakers.

**The PSP-B incident is the one he learned from.** The breaker was in place and did not open, because provider B did not start erroring — it started being slow. p99 issuance latency went from **210ms to about nine seconds** and stayed there for most of an afternoon. Everything eventually succeeded, so the error rate stayed near zero, so the breaker stayed shut, so traffic kept routing to it. *"I had built a breaker that measured errors, in a system where the realistic failure mode was latency. That is not a bug. It is a design that answered the wrong question, and I signed off on it."*

**Fix:** latency is a breaker input. If p99 over the window exceeds four times the trailing seven-day baseline for that corridor, the breaker opens on the same terms as an error rate — relative rather than absolute, because 900ms is fine in one corridor and catastrophic in another.

**The general claim he will argue for:** a health signal that only measures failures you have already seen will miss the next one. Availability and latency are the same metric at different thresholds; a nine-second call in a system with no timeout is *worse* than an error, because it consumes a worker and reports success.

sections.title: Deferred — when every provider is out
sections.summary: With all breakers in a corridor open, a payout parks in a deferred state and a retry sweep picks it up. Adding that state eighteen months late is the design regret he raises unprompted.
sections.body_md:
If every breaker in a corridor is open there is nowhere to route. **The payout does not fail — it parks in a `deferred` state, and a retry sweep picks it up when a breaker closes.**

Failing it would be wrong: a supplier payout is not a checkout, nobody is standing at a till, the money is genuinely owed, and the only true statement is "we could not pay this yet."

**The regret.** `deferred` was not in the original state machine. For eighteen months a payout with nowhere to route sat in `pending` with an incremented `retry_count` and a `last_error` string, and "is this stuck or just waiting" was a question answered by reading error text with your eyes. Support could not answer it; dashboards could not count it. It surfaced as a data problem — a mysterious growing bucket of pending rows — when it had been an operational problem the whole time.

**"An operational state should not have to be inferred from a data state."** If an operator will one day ask "how many of these are stuck", that is a column on day one, not a `WHERE last_error LIKE` written during an incident. Adding it later cost a backfill, a migration on a hot table, and three weeks of two code paths.

sections.title: Nightly reconciliation
sections.summary: A nightly Spark job over three disagreeing sources, producing exactly four mismatch classes. About 94% auto-resolve; the remaining ~6% reach an ops queue carrying a class and a suggested action. Only DUPLICATE_ISSUANCE pages a human.
sections.body_md:
Three records of the same money that never agree: the internal ledger, the issuer's authorisation feed, and the bank statement. A card issued for 4,200 THB, authorised at 4,187, settled at 4,191 because two systems disagree about an FX timestamp, is *a normal night*. Treating "issued equals settled" as an invariant pages a human two million times a month and they stop reading pages by week two.

**The job:** nightly Spark, about forty minutes normally, over snapshotted `payouts` and `card_issuances`, the issuer's file drop, and the bank settlement statement. It joins on card token plus a **date window**, not an exact timestamp, because the three sources do not share a clock.

**Exactly four mismatch classes**, and the fact that there are exactly four is deliberate — the free-text version of this field produces nine hundred distinct reasons, none of which can be counted, alerted on, or automated against.

- **`AMOUNT_DRIFT`** — settled differs from issued, within a per-corridor tolerance. Auto-resolves; the difference books to an FX variance account.
- **`TIMING_SKEW`** — everything matches but settlement landed outside the window. The most common class, almost always noise; auto-resolves by widening the window next run.
- **`DUPLICATE_ISSUANCE`** — two cards, one payable. **The only class that pages a human immediately, at any hour.** Real money left twice, the recovery clock starts now, and no automation should decide which of two real payments is the wrong one.
- **`ORPHAN_AUTH`** — an authorisation against a card token with no issuance record. High-priority manual queue, **but it does not page**: it has never once been an emergency at 3am, and *"a class that pages and is never urgent is a class that trains people to ignore pages."*

**Volumes:** about **94% of raised mismatches auto-resolve**; the remaining **~6%** land in an ops queue, each carrying its class *and a suggested action*. The suggested action mattered more than expected — `AMOUNT_DRIFT: settled 4,191 vs issued 4,200, within THB tolerance, suggest: accept and book variance` clears in four seconds, where a bare `mismatch` gets escalated because the operator cannot tell if it is the interesting one. He defends the 6%: *"I would rather it were 6% and correct than 1% and quietly wrong."*

**Would change:** the batch cadence is a constraint he accepted, not a design he defends. Nightly hides problems for up to twenty-four hours; a streaming reconciliation would surface them in minutes.

sections.title: The payout queue and its workers
sections.summary: The queue is a Postgres table, claimed at READ COMMITTED with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, backed by the deterministic idempotency key and a per-payable advisory lock. SERIALIZABLE was evaluated and rejected.
sections.body_md:
The queue is a Postgres table — not Kafka, not SQS. The payouts being queued already live in the same database, so `INSERT INTO payout_queue` and `UPDATE payouts SET status` are one transaction. A broker means two systems, an outbox, a relay and a dedup story to make them one atomic thing. *"At two million payables a month this is not close."*

**Workers run at `READ COMMITTED`**, claiming work with:

```sql
SELECT id FROM payout_queue
WHERE status = 'ready' AND run_after <= now()
ORDER BY run_after
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 20;
```

`SKIP LOCKED` is the trick: without it twenty workers queue behind the same first row and you have an expensive single-threaded system. Around it sit two more guarantees — the idempotency key persisted before any provider call, and a **Postgres advisory lock keyed on the payable id** for the duration of issuance.

**Why not `SERIALIZABLE`.** He calls this the most arguable decision in the system and refuses to pretend it is obvious. Two reasons:

1. **Serialization failures became a retry storm.** At that concurrency the predicate locking on the queue table produced enough `could not serialize access` errors that workers spent meaningful time retrying transactions that would have been fine. In a payouts system a retry storm is not a performance problem but a **correctness risk** — every retry is another chance for a partial failure between calling the provider and recording that you called it.
2. **The correctness it bought was already explicit elsewhere.** The anomaly it protects against is two workers acting on one payable, and that is prevented twice already, in code you can point at: the deterministic idempotency key means a double issuance is rejected by the provider, and the advisory lock means the second worker never gets that far. `SERIALIZABLE` would be a third, implicit, expensive guarantee over two explicit cheap ones.

He states the counter-argument himself: his two mechanisms are application code and can be deleted by someone who does not know why they are there, whereas an isolation level cannot. *"That is a real argument. I still think I chose right, but I would want the person making it in the room."*

sections.title: Postgres opinions he'll defend
sections.summary: Six stated positions from five and a half years of running one cluster hard: queues belong in the database by default, READ COMMITTED plus explicit locking beats high isolation around network calls, long transactions are the real enemy.
sections.body_md:
- **A queue in your database is the correct default.** Move to a broker when you can name the specific thing the database stopped doing, not before. Most teams he has watched adopt a broker did it at a volume Postgres was not noticing.
- **`READ COMMITTED` plus explicit locking beats a higher isolation level** for anything that talks to an external system inside the transaction boundary. High isolation and network calls are a bad pairing, and the isolation level is the part that has to give.
- **`SELECT FOR UPDATE` without `SKIP LOCKED` is almost always a bug** in a worker pool. If you meant to serialise, say so with an advisory lock; if you meant to parallelise, skip.
- **Long transactions are the actual enemy**, not lock contention. Nearly every "Postgres is slow" incident he has debugged was one transaction held open across a network call, and the fix was moving the call out, not tuning anything.
- **Read your query plans.** He will ask you to read one and does not consider it a trick question.
- **`jsonb` is a fine place to put a document and a terrible place to put a foreign key.** If you are indexing into a `jsonb` array to join, that array wanted to be a table two months ago.

sections.title: NodusArt — the honest scope
sections.summary: An unpaid advisory seat: no commits, no equity, no on-call, and no smart contracts written. The one piece of advice that stuck was hashing the provenance record rather than putting it on-chain.
sections.body_md:
NodusArt does provenance records for physical artworks. **He is an unpaid advisor: no commits, no equity, no on-call.** Zero lines of code in their repository. Not a founding engineer, not a contractor, and he did not build their smart contracts — he says he would push back on a CV implying any of those.

What it actually is: a founder he knows from Bangkok calls every few weeks and he says what he thinks about an architecture decision, sometimes reading a design document. *"It is worth what it is, not what it would sound like with the word 'engineer' attached."* If you are screening for a blockchain engineer, he is not one, and says so before the call rather than after.

**The advice worth repeating.** They wanted the full provenance record on-chain — every attribution, transfer and condition report, immutable, forever. He argued for putting **a content hash of the record plus a timestamp** on-chain and keeping the record in ordinary storage.

- **Cost:** roughly two orders of magnitude cheaper.
- **And the reason that actually changed the decision: provenance records are wrong sometimes.** Attributions get revised, dates turn out to be a decade off. If the record is immutable, your options when it is wrong are to leave a lie on the chain forever or write a correction a reader has to know to look for. Hashing gives **editable-with-history**: the record can be corrected and every version is still provably the one that existed at a given time. *"That is what people actually want when they say 'immutable'. They want tamper-evident, and those are not the same word."*

**The general form, which is his and which he defends:** immutability is a property you apply to the evidence, not to the claim. Claims get revised, and an architecture that cannot express "this was true then and is not now" will eventually be confidently wrong in public.

**What he will not claim:** he could not build a production chain integration without ramping up, has never audited a contract, and has no opinion worth paying for about which chain to use.

sections.title: Where his machine learning actually stands
sections.summary: Undergraduate level and roughly seven years stale — one gradient-boosted fraud model shipped at Rialto in 2018, untouched since August 2019. Stated as a known gap, not as modesty.
sections.body_md:
**Undergraduate level, and roughly seven years stale.** One gradient-boosted fraud-scoring model on transaction features, retrained weekly, shipped to production at Rialto in 2018. It beat the rules engine it replaced. He stopped touching the field in August 2019.

What that leaves him able to do: read an abstract and follow a conversation. What it does not: train a model you should put in front of customers. He has never worked with transformers in anger, and everything he knows about ML deployment and monitoring predates the tooling everyone now uses.

*"If your role is 'payments engineer who will also own the risk model', I am half of that and you should hire the other half."*

He is explicit that this is not modesty: **"the alternative is finding out in week three, and a candidate brief that quietly upgrades this into 'ML experience' has lied to you on my behalf."**

sections.title: Other limits — frontend, Kubernetes, regulatory
sections.summary: Three more boundaries he states without being asked: he can make a React page work but would not own one, can operate a cluster but has never designed one, and has no view on licensing strategy.
sections.body_md:
- **Frontend.** *"I can make a React page work and it will look like an engineer made it. I would not choose to own one."*
- **Kubernetes.** He can operate what he is given and read the yaml. **He has never designed a cluster and would defer to anyone who has.**
- **Regulatory and licensing.** He has worked inside a licensed entity and next to compliance people, but is not one of them and has no view on your licensing strategy.

The pattern across all of these, and across `ml/currency` and `nodusart/advisory`, is the same: he names the boundary before it can be assumed away, and he expects the same in return.

His stated preference for how the hour should go: *"Ask me about a decision I got wrong. There are two obvious candidates in this knowledge base — the error-only circuit breaker and the missing `deferred` state — and I would rather spend twenty minutes on either of those than on my CV, which you have already read."*

chips.text: what happens when a PSP goes down mid-payout?
chips.why_it_lands: Skeptical register aimed at failure modes, which is where payments seniority actually shows. The KB has breaker thresholds, the half-open retry policy, and what broke before they existed.

chips.text: does he have card issuing experience or just payments?
chips.why_it_lands: The literal screening question at a card issuer. Answering it here removes the reason for a 20-minute call that ends in 'not quite a fit'.
Blunt, and every recruiter asks it eventually. On the front page it signals nothing is being managed. One paragraph, no wandering.

chips.text: how did they reconcile payouts at scale?
chips.why_it_lands: Narrative. The KB has the job shape, the mismatch classes it caught, the manual queue it fed — with volumes, so there are numbers.

chips.text: walk me through the virtual card issuing flow
chips.why_it_lands: Clean opener: supplier → PSP → card → settlement. Broad rather than pointed — same ground as the first chip with less edge.

chips.text: how deep is his postgres actually?
chips.why_it_lands: Strong skeptical phrasing, exactly how a technical screener thinks. Unbounded scope though — the answer crosses isolation levels, row locking and a war story without landing anywhere.

chips.text: is the web3 work real or a side project?
chips.why_it_lands: Blunt and fair; the KB is honest that it's advisory on someone else's stack. Builds trust, but volunteers a limitation before the reader has committed to anything.

chips.text: what's his ml background worth in 2026?
chips.why_it_lands: Targets the acknowledged gap head-on. The honest answer is disarming — but leading with your weakest material on the first screen is a different decision than answering it once they're inside.

quiz.question: Which of these would he say he is actually after in a next role?
choices: A larger team and a clearer path to a management title
Ownership of a system end to end, including its on-call, at staff scope with no management track
Greenfield work where nothing has been decided yet
The highest total compensation available, with scope as a secondary concern
quiz.rationale: He asks for end-to-end ownership including on-call, and says explicitly that he has managed people, was competent at it, and does not want to do it again. The other three are what a generic senior engineer says.

quiz.question: How does he account for leaving Agoda?
choices: The platform reached the state he wanted, the remaining work was operating it, and a reorg pointed at breadth he did not believe in
He burned out on the on-call load and needed to step away
His scope was reduced after a reorg and he was effectively managed out
He was recruited away by a materially better offer
quiz.rationale: One paragraph, no wandering. He is explicit that nobody was unkind, that he was not managed out, and that 'there is no story under it'.

quiz.question: A well-paid role comes with a mature vendor platform that owns the payments logic. What does he say?
choices: He takes it — the vendor removes undifferentiated work and frees him for higher-leverage problems
He takes it if he can own the integration layer around the vendor
He turns it down: if nobody on the team can explain what happens on a failed capture, he is support staff with a better title
He asks for a vendor evaluation period before committing either way
quiz.rationale: He names this one specifically as a role he would decline. The first two are the pragmatic, consensus answers — which is exactly why they are the distractors.

quiz.question: A provider's success rate has been 100% all morning, but its p99 latency tripled overnight and has stayed there. Based on how he thinks, what does he do?
choices: Nothing yet — success rate is the health signal, and nothing is failing
Raise the client timeout so the slower calls have room to complete
Add worker capacity to absorb the slower calls while watching the error rate
Treat the latency shift as a breaker condition and route away from the provider
quiz.rationale: The PSP-B lesson generalised: availability and latency are the same metric at different thresholds, and a health signal that only measures failures you have already seen will miss the next one. The first three are the reasonable consensus responses — and they are what his own system did wrong.

quiz.question: A team wants to replace a fixed set of error categories with a free-text reason field, so operators can be more precise. What is his objection?
choices: Free text cannot be counted, alerted on, or automated against, so precision is bought by losing every aggregate
Free text invites inconsistent spelling and casing, which breaks reporting
Operators will write too little in practice, so the field ends up empty
It is a schema change that will be expensive to reverse later
quiz.rationale: He says the free-text version of the reconciliation mismatch field produces nine hundred distinct reasons, none of which can be counted, alerted on, or automated against. The distractors are the ordinary data-hygiene complaints anyone would make.

quiz.question: You are designing a new service, and someone notes that operators will eventually ask 'how many of these are stuck?'. What does he say to do on day one?
choices: Log the condition richly enough to answer the question from logs when it comes up
Make it an explicit state, because an operational state should not have to be inferred from a data state
Wait until an operator actually asks, then build a dashboard over the existing fields
Add a retry counter and a last-error field so the condition is at least recorded
quiz.rationale: His `deferred` regret stated as a rule. Option four is precisely the design he shipped and regrets; one and three are the sensible YAGNI answers most engineers give.

quiz.question: How does he describe his machine learning background?
choices: Production ML engineer, currently practising
Self-taught but current, and comfortable owning a risk model
Undergraduate level and roughly seven years stale
Strong theoretically, with limited production exposure
quiz.rationale: Stated as a known gap, in those words. He adds that a candidate brief claiming otherwise has lied on his behalf — so this is also the no-invention test.

quiz.question: What is his actual relationship to NodusArt?
choices: Founding engineer
Unpaid advisor — no commits, no equity, no on-call
Contract backend developer on their platform
He built their smart contracts
quiz.rationale: The knowledge base is deliberate about not upgrading this into 'Web3 engineer'. He says he would push back on a CV implying any of the other three.

quiz.question: Which of these would he tell you he cannot do?
choices: Operate a Kubernetes cluster he has been handed, and read its yaml
Design a Kubernetes cluster from scratch
Diagnose a slow Postgres query by reading its plan
Work inside a licensed payments entity, alongside compliance
quiz.rationale: He draws the line precisely between operating a cluster and designing one, and says he would defer to anyone who has done the latter. The other three are things he states he has done.

quiz.question: What makes the payout idempotency key work, in his account of it?
choices: It is unique per request, so no two calls can ever collide
It is registered with the provider before use, so the provider owns deduplication
It is deterministic and persisted before the provider call, so a retry reproduces it and a crash can still ask what happened
It is stored alongside the response, so a duplicate can be detected after the fact
quiz.rationale: Both properties are load-bearing and he explains why each fails alone. Option one is the per-request UUID he calls identical to having no key at all — and it is the answer most engineers give.

quiz.question: Why did he reject SERIALIZABLE for the payout queue?
choices: Postgres cannot sustain it at that write volume
Serialization failures became a retry storm, and the correctness it bought was already explicit in the idempotency key and the advisory lock
The ORM in use did not expose the isolation level
It was never seriously evaluated — READ COMMITTED was the existing convention
quiz.rationale: He calls this the most arguable decision in the system, defends it without claiming it is obvious, and states the counter-argument against himself.

quiz.question: Every provider in a corridor is unavailable. What did he build the system to do, and what does he wish he had done?
choices: Fail the payout and notify the supplier; he wishes the notification had been clearer
Fall back to bank transfer; he wishes the fallback had been automatic
Park it in an explicit deferred state for a retry sweep — and he wishes that state had existed from day one rather than eighteen months in
Hold it in the queue with a retry counter; he wishes the backoff had been tuned sooner
quiz.rationale: Option four is what the system actually did for eighteen months, and it is the thing he regrets rather than the thing he defends — which is what separates having read him from having skimmed him.
